content: 1. Two primary approaches to HDV antibody testing have been identified. The first is Universal HDV Antibody Testing, which involves routine testing for HDV antibodies in all individuals with chronic hepatitis B (HBsAg-positive), regardless of their risk factors or clinical characteristics. This ensures that all HBsAg-positive individuals are systematically offered HDV testing services. 2. The second approach is Focused (or Restricted) HDV Antibody Testing, which targets specific populations of HBsAg-positive individuals who are at an increased risk of HDV infection. This risk is determined based on current epidemiological knowledge, risk factors, and clinical characteristics of chronic hepatitis D. High-risk groups include individuals born in regions with high HDV endemicity, people who inject drugs, men who have sex with men, sex workers, individuals co-infected with HCV or HIV, hemodialysis recipients, those reporting high-risk sexual behavior, and individuals with advanced liver disease such as cirrhosis or hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). 3. Until recently, professional societies provided limited guidance on HDV testing and treatment due to gaps in epidemiological knowledge, diagnostic limitations, and the lack of effective and tolerable treatment options. Current professional society guidelines recommend either universal anti-HDV testing for all HBsAg-positive individuals or a focused, risk-based approach targeting high-risk populations or settings. 4. The 2015 WHO guidelines for chronic hepatitis B highlighted HDV testing as part of the initial assessment of HBsAg-positive individuals before therapy but did not make formal recommendations. 5. A PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) question was formulated to guide the development of WHO recommendations on who to test for HDV infection among HBsAg-positive individuals. The question aimed to evaluate the impact, cost, and cost-effectiveness of different testing approaches for detecting HDV serologically in people with chronic hepatitis B. 6. The population of interest includes HBsAg-positive individuals. The interventions considered were universal HDV serology testing for all HBsAg-positive individuals and focused HDV serology testing based on increased risk or advanced liver disease. Comparisons included the standard of care, other testing approaches, or no comparator. Outcomes assessed included the proportion of HBsAg-positive individuals tested for HDV antibodies, the proportion of HDV-positive cases tested for HDV RNA, cost per case diagnosed, incidence of liver-related end-stage disease or mortality, and cost-effectiveness. 7. Systematic review methods were initially employed to design, screen, and select studies from electronic bibliographic databases (MEDLINE, Embase, and Web of Science) for publications between January 2000 and March 2023. However, due to the limited number of studies meeting the PICO criteria, a systematic review was not feasible, and a narrative review of peer-reviewed literature and conference abstracts was conducted instead. 8. Chronic hepatitis D is associated with accelerated progression to cirrhosis and HCC, contributing significantly to morbidity among individuals with hepatitis B. Despite this, no studies directly evaluated the impact, cost, or cost-effectiveness of HDV testing approaches among HBsAg-positive individuals. However, evidence suggests a marked increase in anti-HDV testing and case detection following the implementation of laboratory-based universal reflex anti-HDV testing. 9. Reflex testing involves automatically triggering an anti-HDV test for all individuals who test positive for HBsAg, using a specimen already held in the laboratory. A study in Spain demonstrated a 13-fold increase in anti-HDV testing uptake among HBsAg-positive cases after implementing laboratory-based reflex testing. The absolute number of anti-HDV-positive cases diagnosed increased fivefold, although the prevalence of anti-HDV remained similar before and after reflex testing. 10. While reflex testing can increase HDV testing rates and facilitate universal testing, it requires adequate laboratory capacity and infrastructure, which may not be feasible in lowand middle-income countries. Most hepatitis B testing in these settings is conducted using rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) at the facility level, and anti-HDV testing often requires reference laboratories, limiting the feasibility of direct reflex testing. 11. Currently, RDTs for HDV antibody detection are not commercially available, further restricting clinic-based testing options for HDV. Low rates of HDV antibody testing have been reported in several retrospective cohort studies in high-income countries, indicating that many individuals with chronic hepatitis D likely remain undiagnosed, even in settings where universal testing is recommended. 12. Universal HDV testing has the potential to significantly increase case detection, improve treatment uptake, enhance liver-related disease outcomes, and prevent onward transmission through preventive interventions. It may also improve epidemiological surveillance, support standardized models of care, and reduce stigma among individuals with hepatitis D. 13. However, universal testing requires enhanced laboratory infrastructure and capacity, which may not be feasible in resource-limited settings. Focused (risk-based) testing may be more cost-effective and yield higher testing rates in low-prevalence settings but requires adequate provider knowledge of global HDV epidemiology and affected populations, which is currently limited. 14. Barriers to HDV testing include a lack of patient awareness, stigma associated with high-risk behaviors (e.g., injecting drug use, high-risk sexual behavior), limited access to testing, variable diagnostic performance of HDV assays, and the lack of highly effective and well-tolerated treatment options. 15. Future research priorities include generating high-quality epidemiological data to inform testing approaches, conducting cost-effectiveness and feasibility studies of universal testing in lowand middle-income countries, validating the diagnostic performance of HDV serological and nucleic acid tests, developing anti-HDV RDTs to decentralize testing, and creating fully automated nucleic acid tests for accurate and reliable HDV RNA detection across all genotypes.
